sections.title: Watching the Vocal Tract During Speech

paragraphs.text: **Real-time magnetic resonance imaging (real-time MRI)** records a moving picture of the inside of a person's head and neck while they talk. The view is taken from the side, as if the head were cut straight down the middle from the forehead to the chin, so the face points to the left and the back of the neck is on the right. Air shows up black. Soft tissue such as the tongue, lips, and throat walls shows up in shades of gray and white. This method lets us watch structures move that are normally hidden inside the body.
paragraphs.plain: Real-time magnetic resonance imaging (real-time MRI) records a moving picture of the inside of a person's head and neck while they talk. The view is taken from the side, as if the head were cut straight down the middle from the forehead to the chin, so the face points to the left and the back of the neck is on the right. Air shows up black. Soft tissue such as the tongue, lips, and throat walls shows up in shades of gray and white. This method lets us watch structures move that are normally hidden inside the body.

paragraphs.text: The **lips** sit at the far left edge, and they open, close, round, and spread during speech.
paragraphs.plain: The lips sit at the far left edge, and they open, close, round, and spread during speech.

paragraphs.text: The **tongue** is the large rounded gray mass that fills most of the mouth. It is the most active structure in speech, and it changes shape constantly, bunching up toward the roof of the mouth, pulling back toward the throat, or lying low.
paragraphs.plain: The tongue is the large rounded gray mass that fills most of the mouth. It is the most active structure in speech, and it changes shape constantly, bunching up toward the roof of the mouth, pulling back toward the throat, or lying low.

paragraphs.text: The **roof of the mouth** runs above the tongue. Its front part is the hard, bony **hard palate.** Its back part is the soft, movable **soft palate,** also called the **velum,** which can lift to seal off the nose or lower to let air flow out through the nose.
paragraphs.plain: The roof of the mouth runs above the tongue. Its front part is the hard, bony hard palate. Its back part is the soft, movable soft palate, also called the velum, which can lift to seal off the nose or lower to let air flow out through the nose.

paragraphs.text: Behind the tongue, a dark vertical channel of air runs down the throat. This is the **pharynx.** Below it sits the **larynx,** which holds the **vocal folds,** and behind all of it the bright vertical column of the spine runs down the right side of the image.
paragraphs.plain: Behind the tongue, a dark vertical channel of air runs down the throat. This is the pharynx. Below it sits the larynx, which holds the vocal folds, and behind all of it the bright vertical column of the spine runs down the right side of the image.

paragraphs.text: When a person speaks, all of these structures move at the same time and at high speed. The jaw rises and falls, the lips open and close, the tongue reshapes itself many times per second, and the soft palate lifts and lowers. Each sound we make depends on a precise shape of this whole passage, and the shapes follow one another smoothly rather than one at a time. The two MRI movies capture the same speaker's vocal tract in two different shapes, and the difference between them comes almost entirely from where the tongue and lips are placed.

sections.title: How Speech and Reading Are Learned

paragraphs.text: We learn to move our speech organs in extremely complex ways with no instructions and with almost no visual feedback. Nobody tells a young child where to place the tongue tip for a particular sound or how high to lift the back of the tongue. A child also cannot see their own tongue, soft palate, or vocal folds, since these are hidden inside the mouth and throat in exactly the way the MRI images reveal. Even so, children master these movements.
paragraphs.plain: We learn to move our speech organs in extremely complex ways with no instructions and with almost no visual feedback. Nobody tells a young child where to place the tongue tip for a particular sound or how high to lift the back of the tongue. A child also cannot see their own tongue, soft palate, or vocal folds, since these are hidden inside the mouth and throat in exactly the way the MRI images reveal. Even so, children master these movements.

paragraphs.text: **By ages 2 to 4,** children speak with a wide vocabulary and with language that is close to adult language. This happens with hardly any explicit instruction. Children are not given lessons in grammar or pronunciation at this age, yet they pick up thousands of words and the rules for putting them together just from being around people who talk.

Children are not given lessons in grammar or pronunciation at this age, yet they pick up thousands of words and the rules for putting them together just from being around people who talk.

paragraphs.text: **Reading and writing** follow a very different path. A child may memorize the visual shapes of the letters of the alphabet fairly early. Reading and writing whole words, though, usually comes at **ages 6 to 7,** and it requires a great deal of instruction.

paragraphs.text: The contrast is striking. Speech involves hidden organs that the learner cannot see, yet it develops almost on its own.

paragraphs.text: Reading and writing involve the eyes and hands, which are fully visible, yet they need years of deliberate teaching.

paragraphs.text: This difference shows that speech is a deep human cognitive skill that the brain is prepared to acquire, while literacy is a learned tool built on top of it.

paragraphs.text: **Articulatory phonetics** is the field that studies the movements of the different structures of the vocal tract. The **vocal tract** is the full air passage used in speech, running from the larynx up through the throat and mouth to the lips, with a side branch into the nose. Articulatory phonetics asks which structures move, where they move to, and how those movements create the different sounds of a language. Real-time MRI is one of the main tools of this field, since it lets researchers measure the tongue, lips, and soft palate directly while a person talks.

The vocal tract is the full air passage used in speech, running from the larynx up through the throat and mouth to the lips, with a side branch into the nose. Articulatory phonetics asks which structures move, where they move to, and how those movements create the different sounds of a language. Real-time MRI is one of the main tools of this field, since it lets researchers measure the tongue, lips, and soft palate directly while a person talks.

paragraphs.text: In just the **last two years, voice assistants** and other **speech technology** have come to **emulate** human speech ability in ways that almost no one thought possible. To emulate an ability means to reproduce its behavior. These systems can now produce speech that sounds natural and humanlike, and they can recognize and respond to spoken language with high accuracy.

To emulate an ability means to reproduce its behavior. These systems can now produce speech that sounds natural and humanlike, and they can recognize and respond to spoken language with high accuracy.

paragraphs.text: **LING 285 is about both human speech and AI speech.** One side of the course studies how people physically produce and perceive speech. The other side studies how modern AI systems model that same ability, so the human skill and the machine version can be compared directly.

sections.title: The Vocal Tract as a Vibrating Tube of Air

paragraphs.text: The next step in understanding speech is to focus not on the tongue and lips themselves but on the **air** that fills the space between the tongue and the rest of the vocal tract. In the real vocal tract, that air space bends: it runs down the throat and then turns forward through the mouth. If we ignore that curve and straighten the passage out, the vocal tract becomes a simple **tube of air.**
paragraphs.plain: The next step in understanding speech is to focus not on the tongue and lips themselves but on the air that fills the space between the tongue and the rest of the vocal tract. In the real vocal tract, that air space bends: it runs down the throat and then turns forward through the mouth. If we ignore that curve and straighten the passage out, the vocal tract becomes a simple tube of air.

paragraphs.text: One end of the tube corresponds to the **lips,** where the passage is open to the outside air.
paragraphs.plain: One end of the tube corresponds to the lips, where the passage is open to the outside air.

paragraphs.text: The other end corresponds to the **larynx** deep in the throat, where the tube is treated as closed.
paragraphs.plain: The other end corresponds to the larynx deep in the throat, where the tube is treated as closed.

paragraphs.text: The walls of the tube stand for the tongue and the other surfaces that surround the air space.
paragraphs.plain: The walls of the tube stand for the tongue and the other surfaces that surround the air space.

paragraphs.text: The tube is labeled **schwa.** Schwa is the neutral, relaxed vowel sound, the "uh" sound in the first syllable of "about" or the last syllable of "sofa." For schwa, the tongue sits in a central resting position and does not narrow the passage much anywhere, so the air space is close to the same width from end to end. That makes schwa the vowel that fits the straight, even tube best.
paragraphs.plain: The tube is labeled schwa. Schwa is the neutral, relaxed vowel sound, the "uh" sound in the first syllable of "about" or the last syllable of "sofa." For schwa, the tongue sits in a central resting position and does not narrow the passage much anywhere, so the air space is close to the same width from end to end. That makes schwa the vowel that fits the straight, even tube best.

paragraphs.text: Inside the tube, the air is drawn as many small blue circles arranged in vertical columns, and each circle stands for a small bit of air. When the tube vibrates, these bits of air do not travel down the tube and out the end. Instead, each column shifts back and forth around its own resting position.
paragraphs.plain: Inside the tube, the air is drawn as many small blue circles arranged in vertical columns, and each circle stands for a small bit of air. When the tube vibrates, these bits of air do not travel down the tube and out the end. Instead, each column shifts back and forth around its own resting position.

paragraphs.text: As neighboring columns move toward each other, the air in that region is squeezed together into a **compression,** where the air is packed more tightly.
paragraphs.plain: As neighboring columns move toward each other, the air in that region is squeezed together into a compression, where the air is packed more tightly.

paragraphs.text: As neighboring columns move away from each other, the air in that region spreads out into a **rarefaction,** where the air is packed more loosely.
paragraphs.plain: As neighboring columns move away from each other, the air in that region spreads out into a rarefaction, where the air is packed more loosely.

paragraphs.text: These regions of packing and spreading move along the tube and reflect back from its ends, and this repeating pattern is the **vibration of air** that makes up the sound of the vowel.
paragraphs.plain: These regions of packing and spreading move along the tube and reflect back from its ends, and this repeating pattern is the vibration of air that makes up the sound of the vowel.

paragraphs.text: **Acoustic phonetics** is the field that studies exactly this: how air vibrates in the vocal tract and what sound those vibrations produce. Articulatory phonetics describes the shape of the tube, and acoustic phonetics describes the physics of the air inside it. The two fields connect directly, since changing the tongue and lip positions changes the shape of the tube, and changing the shape of the tube changes how the air inside it vibrates.

sections.title: Harms, Benefits, and the Problem of Understanding AI

paragraphs.text: AI brings real **psychological, economic, social, and environmental harms.** Given everything known about these harms, it is tempting to simply ignore AI and act as if it did not exist. Many scientists also warn about **existential harm,** meaning the possibility that advanced AI could threaten humanity's survival or basic way of life. Even with that warning, pretending AI does not exist is not a workable option.

Many scientists also warn about existential harm, meaning the possibility that advanced AI could threaten humanity's survival or basic way of life. Even with that warning, pretending AI does not exist is not a workable option.

paragraphs.text: AI exists, and it comes with many harms and also some benefits. Two examples of benefits are **immunotherapy,** a medical approach that uses the body's own immune system to fight diseases such as cancer, and **environmental engineering,** the design of solutions to environmental problems.

paragraphs.text: The environmental case cuts both ways, as captured by a newspaper headline asking, **"Will A.I. Ruin the Planet or Save the Planet?"**
paragraphs.plain: The environmental case cuts both ways, as captured by a newspaper headline asking, "Will A.I. Ruin the Planet or Save the Planet?"

paragraphs.text: Running large AI systems uses enormous amounts of energy, which is one of the environmental harms, while AI tools are also being applied to engineering problems that could help the environment.

paragraphs.text: One of the biggest dangers of AI is that **we have no idea how it works.** This is summed up in the phrase **"We know everything, and understand nothing."**

paragraphs.text: "We know everything" means that every number and every calculation inside an AI system is available to be inspected, since people built the system and can look at all of its parts.

paragraphs.text: "We understand nothing" means that, even with all of those details in hand, no one can explain why the system produces the particular answers it does or what it is really doing when it produces them.

paragraphs.text: The number of people who **know** how these systems operate is very, very small. That concentration of knowledge is a danger in itself, since the decisions about how AI is built and used end up in very few hands.

paragraphs.text: **AI literacy,** meaning a working understanding of what AI systems are and how they behave, is necessary for many groups of people. Scientists who use AI need it to judge whether their results are trustworthy. Politicians who need to control AI need it to write sensible rules. Lawyers who litigate cases involving AI need it to argue about what a system did and why.

sections.title: Diotima's Ladder and What Is Valued in 2026

paragraphs.text: **Diotima,** dated here to around 440 **BCE,** is the teacher who, in Plato's dialogue the Symposium, teaches **Socrates** about a ladder of ascent. The ladder describes how a person climbs from ordinary, surface-level knowledge of particular things toward deeper understanding of the general ideas behind them. A chain of teachers runs from her through Greek philosophy: Diotima taught Socrates, Socrates taught **Plato,** and Plato taught **Aristotle.** The large marble bust represents Diotima, and the three smaller portraits below her represent Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle in that order.
paragraphs.plain: Diotima, dated here to around 440 BCE, is the teacher who, in Plato's dialogue the Symposium, teaches Socrates about a ladder of ascent. The ladder describes how a person climbs from ordinary, surface-level knowledge of particular things toward deeper understanding of the general ideas behind them. A chain of teachers runs from her through Greek philosophy: Diotima taught Socrates, Socrates taught Plato, and Plato taught Aristotle. The large marble bust represents Diotima, and the three smaller portraits below her represent Socrates, Plato, and Aristotle in that order.

paragraphs.text: The **bottom of the ladder** holds the kinds of knowledge and skill that come from routine and from copying what already exists.
paragraphs.plain: The bottom of the ladder holds the kinds of knowledge and skill that come from routine and from copying what already exists.

paragraphs.text: These include **daily experience, habit,** and **memorization,** along with **specialized skills, repetition and replication,** and learning from **textbooks.**
paragraphs.plain: These include daily experience, habit, and memorization, along with specialized skills, repetition and replication, and learning from textbooks.

paragraphs.text: Thinking at this level follows the rule that **similar is same, and slight difference is different.** Things that look alike on the surface are treated as identical, and things that look even a little different on the surface are treated as unrelated.
paragraphs.plain: Thinking at this level follows the rule that similar is same, and slight difference is different. Things that look alike on the surface are treated as identical, and things that look even a little different on the surface are treated as unrelated.

paragraphs.text: The **top of the ladder** holds **creativity, insight, thought, focus, attention, imagination, and vision,** along with **problem-posing, problem-solving, critical reading, and creative writing.**
paragraphs.plain: The top of the ladder holds creativity, insight, thought, focus, attention, imagination, and vision, along with problem-posing, problem-solving, critical reading, and creative writing.

paragraphs.text: Thinking at this level follows a reversed rule: **different can be same, and similar can be different.** Things that look different on the surface can share the same deeper structure, and things that look alike on the surface can turn out to be fundamentally different.
paragraphs.plain: Thinking at this level follows a reversed rule: different can be same, and similar can be different. Things that look different on the surface can share the same deeper structure, and things that look alike on the surface can turn out to be fundamentally different.

paragraphs.text: Speech gives a direct example. The sounds f and v sound different, yet they are made in the same place in the mouth, so in that respect they are the same. The th in "thing" and the th in "that" are spelled identically, yet one uses vocal fold vibration and the other does not, so they are different sounds.
paragraphs.plain: Speech gives a direct example. The sounds f and v sound different, yet they are made in the same place in the mouth, so in that respect they are the same. The th in "thing" and the th in "that" are spelled identically, yet one uses vocal fold vibration and the other does not, so they are different sounds.

paragraphs.text: **Problem-posing** means asking good questions in the first place, which is separate from **problem-solving,** which means answering questions once they have been asked.
paragraphs.plain: Problem-posing means asking good questions in the first place, which is separate from problem-solving, which means answering questions once they have been asked.

paragraphs.text: A person climbs the ladder through repeated cycles of **question and answer.** Each cycle of asking a question and working out an answer lifts understanding one rung higher, and the cycles repeat again and again on the way from the bottom to the top. This is the method Socrates became famous for, and it traces back to Diotima's teaching of him.

Each cycle of asking a question and working out an answer lifts understanding one rung higher, and the cycles repeat again and again on the way from the bottom to the top. This is the method Socrates became famous for, and it traces back to Diotima's teaching of him.

paragraphs.text: For about 2500 **years,** people could fake it. They could do well in school and at work without ever climbing the ladder, simply by memorizing, repeating, and replicating. In 2026 that is no longer true. In interviews for jobs and for graduate school, what matters now is whether a person shows the properties at the **top of Diotima's ladder,** such as creativity, insight, problem-posing, and the ability to see when different things are the same and similar things are different.

sections.title: Learning Speech by Doing: Voice and Place of Articulation

paragraphs.text: The quickest way to understand speech sounds is to produce them and pay attention to what the body does. The exercise uses four pairs of sounds, and each pair is held out as one long continuous sound that switches partway through from the first sound to the second.
paragraphs.plain: The quickest way to understand speech sounds is to produce them and pay attention to what the body does. The exercise uses four pairs of sounds, and each pair is held out as one long continuous sound that switches partway through from the first sound to the second.

paragraphs.text: The first pair is **f then v.** Say the f in "fat" and hold it, then switch to the v in "vat" and hold that.
paragraphs.plain: The first pair is f then v. Say the f in "fat" and hold it, then switch to the v in "vat" and hold that.

paragraphs.text: The second pair is **th then th.** Say the th in "thing" and hold it, then switch to the th in "that" and hold that.
paragraphs.plain: The second pair is th then th. Say the th in "thing" and hold it, then switch to the th in "that" and hold that.

paragraphs.text: The third pair is **s then z.** Say the s in "sing" and hold it, then switch to the z in "zing" and hold that.
paragraphs.plain: The third pair is s then z. Say the s in "sing" and hold it, then switch to the z in "zing" and hold that.

paragraphs.text: The fourth pair is **sh then j.** Say the sh in "mesh" and hold it, then switch to the sound written j here, which is the sound in the middle of "beige." This is the soft buzzing sound, not the j in "jump."
paragraphs.plain: The fourth pair is sh then j. Say the sh in "mesh" and hold it, then switch to the sound written j here, which is the sound in the middle of "beige." This is the soft buzzing sound, not the j in "jump."

paragraphs.text: The first question is what changes between the first and second sound of each pair. Resting the fingers lightly on the front of the throat while switching makes the change easy to feel.
paragraphs.plain: The first question is what changes between the first and second sound of each pair. Resting the fingers lightly on the front of the throat while switching makes the change easy to feel.

paragraphs.text: During f, the first th, s, and sh, the throat stays still and the sound is a pure hiss of air.
paragraphs.plain: During f, the first th, s, and sh, the throat stays still and the sound is a pure hiss of air.

paragraphs.text: During v, the second th, z, and the sound in "beige," a buzzing vibration appears in the throat and the sound gains a humming quality.
paragraphs.plain: During v, the second th, z, and the sound in "beige," a buzzing vibration appears in the throat and the sound gains a humming quality.

paragraphs.text: The difference is **voice,** which is whether the **vocal folds** vibrate or not. The vocal folds are two small folds of tissue inside the larynx. When they are held apart, air passes through silently and the sound is **voiceless.** When they are brought close together, the air flowing between them makes them vibrate rapidly, and the sound is **voiced.**
paragraphs.plain: The difference is voice, which is whether the vocal folds vibrate or not. The vocal folds are two small folds of tissue inside the larynx. When they are held apart, air passes through silently and the sound is voiceless. When they are brought close together, the air flowing between them makes them vibrate rapidly, and the sound is voiced.

paragraphs.text: Within each pair, the tongue and lips stay in the same position the whole time. Only the vocal folds change, which shows that voicing is controlled separately from the mouth.
paragraphs.plain: Within each pair, the tongue and lips stay in the same position the whole time. Only the vocal folds change, which shows that voicing is controlled separately from the mouth.

paragraphs.text: The second question is what changes from one line to the next, meaning from the f and v pair to the th pair to the s and z pair to the sh pair.
paragraphs.plain: The second question is what changes from one line to the next, meaning from the f and v pair to the th pair to the s and z pair to the sh pair.

paragraphs.text: For f and v, the lower lip presses lightly against the upper front teeth.
paragraphs.plain: For f and v, the lower lip presses lightly against the upper front teeth.

paragraphs.text: For both th sounds, the tip of the tongue touches the upper front teeth.
paragraphs.plain: For both th sounds, the tip of the tongue touches the upper front teeth.

paragraphs.text: For s and z, the tip of the tongue comes close to the ridge just behind the upper front teeth.
paragraphs.plain: For s and z, the tip of the tongue comes close to the ridge just behind the upper front teeth.

paragraphs.text: For sh and the sound in "beige," the tongue pulls a bit further back, behind that ridge.
paragraphs.plain: For sh and the sound in "beige," the tongue pulls a bit further back, behind that ridge.

paragraphs.text: The difference is **place of articulation,** which is the location in the vocal tract where the narrowing that makes the sound is formed. Moving from one line to the next moves that narrowing steadily further back in the mouth.
paragraphs.plain: The difference is place of articulation, which is the location in the vocal tract where the narrowing that makes the sound is formed. Moving from one line to the next moves that narrowing steadily further back in the mouth.

paragraphs.text: Voice and place of articulation are two separate, independent properties of a speech sound. Every sound in this exercise can be described by stating both of them, and changing one while keeping the other fixed produces a different sound.

paragraphs.text: All of the sounds in the exercise belong to a group called **fricatives.** A fricative is made by bringing two parts of the vocal tract very close together without closing the passage completely. Air pushed from the lungs is forced through the narrow gap, and passing through such a small opening makes the air flow turbulent and chaotic. That turbulent flow produces the hissing or buzzing noise that is typical of fricatives, and the sound can be held for as long as there is breath.

paragraphs.text: The English fricatives are organized in a table by **voice** in the rows and **place of articulation** in the columns.

paragraphs.text: **Labial Dental Alveolar Postalveolar**
paragraphs.plain: Labial Dental Alveolar Postalveolar

paragraphs.text: **Voiceless** f th s sh
paragraphs.plain: Voiceless f th s sh

paragraphs.text: **Voiced** v th z j

paragraphs.text: Each column is a place of articulation, and each column contains one voiceless and one voiced fricative made in that same place.

paragraphs.text: **Labial** means made with the lips. For f and v, the lower lip rises to lightly touch the upper front teeth, and the air hisses through the gaps between them. Real- time MRI of these sounds shows the lower lip tucked up under the upper teeth while the tongue lies relatively low and relaxed in the mouth.

Real- time MRI of these sounds shows the lower lip tucked up under the upper teeth while the tongue lies relatively low and relaxed in the mouth.

paragraphs.text: **Dental** means made at the teeth. For the th in "thing" and the th in "that," the tip of the tongue touches or rests just between the upper front teeth. The MRI of these sounds shows the front of the tongue pushed forward right up to the teeth.

paragraphs.text: **Alveolar** means made at the **alveolar ridge,** the small bony ridge on the roof of the mouth just behind the upper front teeth. For s and z, the tongue tip rises to form a narrow groove close to that ridge. The MRI shows the tongue tip raised toward the front of the roof of the mouth, a short distance behind the teeth.

For s and z, the tongue tip rises to form a narrow groove close to that ridge. The MRI shows the tongue tip raised toward the front of the roof of the mouth, a short distance behind the teeth.

paragraphs.text: **Postalveolar** means made just behind the alveolar ridge. For sh and the sound in "beige," a wider section of the front of the tongue rises toward the roof of the mouth a little further back than for s. The MRI shows the raised part of the tongue shifted backward compared with s, and the lips often push slightly forward during these sounds.

paragraphs.text: Each row is a voicing category. The top row holds the **voiceless** fricatives, made with the vocal folds apart and still. The bottom row holds the **voiced** fricatives, made with the vocal folds vibrating. Two fricatives in the same column differ only in voicing, and two fricatives in the same row differ only in place of articulation. The two th sounds make the point sharply, since English spells them the same way even though one is voiceless and the other is voiced.

The bottom row holds the voiced fricatives, made with the vocal folds vibrating. Two fricatives in the same column differ only in voicing, and two fricatives in the same row differ only in place of articulation. The two th sounds make the point sharply, since English spells them the same way even though one is voiceless and the other is voiced.

paragraphs.text: **Stops** are made differently from fricatives. For a stop, two parts of the vocal tract come together and **close the passage completely,** so that for a brief moment air cannot escape through the mouth at all.
paragraphs.plain: Stops are made differently from fricatives. For a stop, two parts of the vocal tract come together and close the passage completely, so that for a brief moment air cannot escape through the mouth at all.

paragraphs.text: While the closure is held, air coming up from the lungs keeps pushing into the mouth, and the air pressure builds up behind the closure.
paragraphs.plain: While the closure is held, air coming up from the lungs keeps pushing into the mouth, and the air pressure builds up behind the closure.

paragraphs.text: When the closure is released, the trapped air bursts out suddenly, and that burst is part of what makes a stop sound short and sharp.
paragraphs.plain: When the closure is released, the trapped air bursts out suddenly, and that burst is part of what makes a stop sound short and sharp.

paragraphs.text: Unlike a fricative, a stop cannot be held as a continuous sound, since the sound depends on the closing and the release.
paragraphs.plain: Unlike a fricative, a stop cannot be held as a continuous sound, since the sound depends on the closing and the release.

paragraphs.text: The English stops fall into a grid of three places of articulation and three types. Real-time MRI movies capture each of these nine sounds in the middle of its closure.
paragraphs.plain: The English stops fall into a grid of three places of articulation and three types. Real-time MRI movies capture each of these nine sounds in the middle of its closure.

paragraphs.text: The first row is **p, b, and m,** and all three are made by closing the **lips.**
paragraphs.plain: The first row is p, b, and m, and all three are made by closing the lips.

paragraphs.text: For p, the lips press together, the vocal folds stay still, and the release produces a voiceless puff of air.
paragraphs.plain: For p, the lips press together, the vocal folds stay still, and the release produces a voiceless puff of air.

paragraphs.text: For b, the lips close in the same way, but the vocal folds vibrate, so b is voiced.
paragraphs.plain: For b, the lips close in the same way, but the vocal folds vibrate, so b is voiced.

paragraphs.text: For m, the lips close in the same way and the vocal folds vibrate, but the **soft palate lowers.** This opens the passage into the nose, so air flows out through the nose the whole time the lips are closed. A sound made this way is called a **nasal,** and the MRI of m shows the gap opened between the soft palate and the back of the throat.
paragraphs.plain: For m, the lips close in the same way and the vocal folds vibrate, but the soft palate lowers. This opens the passage into the nose, so air flows out through the nose the whole time the lips are closed. A sound made this way is called a nasal, and the MRI of m shows the gap opened between the soft palate and the back of the throat.

paragraphs.text: The second row is **t, d, and n,** and all three are made by pressing the tip of the tongue against the **alveolar ridge,** the same place used for s and z.
paragraphs.plain: The second row is t, d, and n, and all three are made by pressing the tip of the tongue against the alveolar ridge, the same place used for s and z.

paragraphs.text: For t, the tongue tip seals against the ridge and the vocal folds stay still, so t is voiceless.
paragraphs.plain: For t, the tongue tip seals against the ridge and the vocal folds stay still, so t is voiceless.

paragraphs.text: For d, the tongue tip seals in the same place and the vocal folds vibrate, so d is voiced.
paragraphs.plain: For d, the tongue tip seals in the same place and the vocal folds vibrate, so d is voiced.

paragraphs.text: For n, the tongue tip seals in the same place, the vocal folds vibrate, and the soft palate lowers so air escapes through the nose, which makes n a nasal. The MRI images of this row show the front of the tongue raised and pressed against the roof of the mouth just behind the teeth.
paragraphs.plain: For n, the tongue tip seals in the same place, the vocal folds vibrate, and the soft palate lowers so air escapes through the nose, which makes n a nasal. The MRI images of this row show the front of the tongue raised and pressed against the roof of the mouth just behind the teeth.

paragraphs.text: The third row is **k, g, and ng,** and all three are made by raising the **back of the tongue** against the **soft palate** at the back of the roof of the mouth.
paragraphs.plain: The third row is k, g, and ng, and all three are made by raising the back of the tongue against the soft palate at the back of the roof of the mouth.

paragraphs.text: For k, the back of the tongue seals against the soft palate and the vocal folds stay still, so k is voiceless.
paragraphs.plain: For k, the back of the tongue seals against the soft palate and the vocal folds stay still, so k is voiceless.

paragraphs.text: For g, the seal is in the same place and the vocal folds vibrate, so g is voiced.
paragraphs.plain: For g, the seal is in the same place and the vocal folds vibrate, so g is voiced.

paragraphs.text: For ng, the sound at the end of "sing," the seal is in the same place, the vocal folds vibrate, and the passage to the nose opens so air flows out through the nose. The MRI images of this row show the tongue bunched upward and backward, meeting the roof of the mouth far back near the throat, while the lips and tongue tip stay out of the way.
paragraphs.plain: For ng, the sound at the end of "sing," the seal is in the same place, the vocal folds vibrate, and the passage to the nose opens so air flows out through the nose. The MRI images of this row show the tongue bunched upward and backward, meeting the roof of the mouth far back near the throat, while the lips and tongue tip stay out of the way.

paragraphs.text: The columns of the grid follow the same logic as the fricative table. The first column, **p, t, and k,** holds the **voiceless** stops. The second column, **b, d, and g,** holds the **voiced** stops. The third column, **m, n, and ng,** holds the **nasal** stops, which are voiced and send air through the nose. Reading down a column changes only the place of articulation, from the lips to the alveolar ridge to the soft palate. Reading across a row keeps the place fixed and changes only voicing and whether the nose is open. Nine different sounds come from combining just three places of closure with three settings of the vocal folds and soft palate, which shows how a small number of independent movements builds a large set of speech sounds.

sections.title: Watching Speech Inside the Vocal Tract

paragraphs.text: **Real-time** MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) lets us film the inside of the head while a person is talking. The images are **midsagittal,** which means they are a side-view slice taken straight down the middle of the head, from the nose to the back of the neck. The face points to the left, so the lips are on the left edge and the spinal column is the bright vertical band on the right. The recordings run for about half a minute each and include the sound of the speaker, so every movement can be matched to the speech it produces.
paragraphs.plain: Real-time MRI (magnetic resonance imaging) lets us film the inside of the head while a person is talking. The images are midsagittal, which means they are a side-view slice taken straight down the middle of the head, from the nose to the back of the neck. The face points to the left, so the lips are on the left edge and the spinal column is the bright vertical band on the right. The recordings run for about half a minute each and include the sound of the speaker, so every movement can be matched to the speech it produces.

paragraphs.text: In MRI, **air shows up black** because it gives off almost no signal, and soft tissue like the tongue shows up gray or white. The dark spaces in the image are therefore the open airways: the mouth cavity, the nasal passages above the roof of the mouth, and the **pharynx,** which is the air tube at the back of the throat behind the tongue.
paragraphs.plain: In MRI, air shows up black because it gives off almost no signal, and soft tissue like the tongue shows up gray or white. The dark spaces in the image are therefore the open airways: the mouth cavity, the nasal passages above the roof of the mouth, and the pharynx, which is the air tube at the back of the throat behind the tongue.

paragraphs.text: The large rounded gray mass filling most of the mouth is the **tongue.** Above it is the **hard palate,** the bony roof of the mouth, and hanging down from the back of the hard palate is the **velum,** or soft palate, which can be raised or lowered to close or open the path from the throat into the nose.
paragraphs.plain: The large rounded gray mass filling most of the mouth is the tongue. Above it is the hard palate, the bony roof of the mouth, and hanging down from the back of the hard palate is the velum, or soft palate, which can be raised or lowered to close or open the path from the throat into the nose.

paragraphs.text: When these recordings play, the tongue, lips, jaw, and velum are all moving at once and very quickly. Every consonant and vowel we hear is the result of the speaker shaping this tube of air in a particular way. **Phonetics** is the study of these speech sounds, and the images give us a direct way to see the shapes behind them.

Every consonant and vowel we hear is the result of the speaker shaping this tube of air in a particular way. Phonetics is the study of these speech sounds, and the images give us a direct way to see the shapes behind them.

paragraphs.text: A **fricative** is a consonant made by bringing two parts of the mouth very close together without closing them completely. Air is pushed through that narrow gap, and the squeezed air becomes turbulent, which produces the hissing or buzzing noise we hear in sounds like f and s. A fricative can be held for as long as we have breath, which is different from sounds that require a full closure.
paragraphs.plain: A fricative is a consonant made by bringing two parts of the mouth very close together without closing them completely. Air is pushed through that narrow gap, and the squeezed air becomes turbulent, which produces the hissing or buzzing noise we hear in sounds like f and s. A fricative can be held for as long as we have breath, which is different from sounds that require a full closure.

paragraphs.text: English fricatives are organized along two dimensions: **place of articulation** and **voicing.** Place of articulation is where in the mouth the narrow gap is formed. Voicing is whether the **vocal folds** in the larynx are vibrating while the sound is made.
paragraphs.plain: English fricatives are organized along two dimensions: place of articulation and voicing. Place of articulation is where in the mouth the narrow gap is formed. Voicing is whether the vocal folds in the larynx are vibrating while the sound is made.

paragraphs.text: A **voiceless** sound is made with the vocal folds apart and not vibrating, so the only noise is the hiss of air through the gap.
paragraphs.plain: A voiceless sound is made with the vocal folds apart and not vibrating, so the only noise is the hiss of air through the gap.

paragraphs.text: A **voiced** sound is made with the vocal folds vibrating, so the hiss is combined with a buzz. Placing a hand on the throat while saying "ssss" and then "zzzz" makes the difference easy to feel, since only the second produces vibration.
paragraphs.plain: A voiced sound is made with the vocal folds vibrating, so the hiss is combined with a buzz. Placing a hand on the throat while saying "ssss" and then "zzzz" makes the difference easy to feel, since only the second produces vibration.

paragraphs.text: The English fricatives fall into **four places of articulation,** and each place has a voiceless and a voiced member.
paragraphs.plain: The English fricatives fall into four places of articulation, and each place has a voiceless and a voiced member.

paragraphs.text: **Labial** fricatives are f (voiceless) and v (voiced). The word labial refers to the lips, and for f and v the lower lip is raised up against the upper front teeth.
paragraphs.plain: Labial fricatives are f (voiceless) and v (voiced). The word labial refers to the lips, and for f and v the lower lip is raised up against the upper front teeth.

paragraphs.text: **Dental** fricatives are both spelled th. The voiceless one is the sound at the start of "think," and the voiced one is the sound at the start of "this." The tip of the tongue is placed against or just between the upper teeth.
paragraphs.plain: Dental fricatives are both spelled th. The voiceless one is the sound at the start of "think," and the voiced one is the sound at the start of "this." The tip of the tongue is placed against or just between the upper teeth.

paragraphs.text: **Alveolar** fricatives are s (voiceless) and z (voiced). The **alveolar ridge** is the bony ridge just behind the upper front teeth, and the tongue tip is raised close to it.
paragraphs.plain: Alveolar fricatives are s (voiceless) and z (voiced). The alveolar ridge is the bony ridge just behind the upper front teeth, and the tongue tip is raised close to it.

paragraphs.text: **Postalveolar** fricatives are sh (voiceless) and the voiced partner symbolized as j, which is the sound in the middle of "measure" and "vision." The narrow gap is formed just behind the alveolar ridge, a little farther back in the mouth than for s and z.

paragraphs.text: The four MRI images line up with these four places, and they show how the constriction moves backward from one place to the next.

paragraphs.text: The pairing matters: f and v, the two th sounds, s and z, and sh and its voiced partner are each made with the **same place and the same manner.** The only thing that separates the members of each pair is whether the vocal folds are vibrating.

paragraphs.text: A **stop** is a consonant made by closing the vocal tract completely at some point so that air cannot get out through the mouth. Air pressure builds up behind the closure, and when the closure is released, the trapped air bursts out. English has two kinds of stops, **oral stops** and **nasal stops.**
paragraphs.plain: A stop is a consonant made by closing the vocal tract completely at some point so that air cannot get out through the mouth. Air pressure builds up behind the closure, and when the closure is released, the trapped air bursts out. English has two kinds of stops, oral stops and nasal stops.

paragraphs.text: In an **oral stop,** also called a **plosive,** the velum is raised and presses against the back wall of the throat, which seals off the nose. With both the mouth and the nose closed, pressure builds and is released as a small burst of air.
paragraphs.plain: In an oral stop, also called a plosive, the velum is raised and presses against the back wall of the throat, which seals off the nose. With both the mouth and the nose closed, pressure builds and is released as a small burst of air.

paragraphs.text: In a **nasal stop,** the mouth is closed in exactly the same way, but the velum is lowered. Air flows up and out through the nose the whole time, so there is no pressure build-up, and the sound has a humming quality.
paragraphs.plain: In a nasal stop, the mouth is closed in exactly the same way, but the velum is lowered. Air flows up and out through the nose the whole time, so there is no pressure build-up, and the sound has a humming quality.

paragraphs.text: The stops are grouped into **three places of articulation,** and each place has a voiceless oral stop, a voiced oral stop, and a nasal stop.
paragraphs.plain: The stops are grouped into three places of articulation, and each place has a voiceless oral stop, a voiced oral stop, and a nasal stop.

paragraphs.text: At the **lips,** p is voiceless, b is voiced, and m is the nasal. The MRI images for p, b, and m all show the two lips pressed together, closing off the front of the mouth.

paragraphs.text: At the **alveolar ridge,** t is voiceless, d is voiced, and n is the nasal. The images for t, d, and n show the tip of the tongue raised and pressed against the ridge behind the upper teeth.

paragraphs.text: At the **velum,** k is voiceless, g is voiced, and ng is the nasal, which is the sound at the end of "sing." A sound made at the velum is called **velar.** The images for k, g, and ng show the back of the tongue humped up and pressed against the soft palate.

paragraphs.text: The nasal images differ from the oral images in the position of the velum. In m, n, and ng, the velum hangs down away from the back of the throat, leaving an open passage into the nose, while in p, t, and k the velum is raised to seal that passage. The short video clips of each stop show the closure forming and releasing in real time, which makes it clear that a stop is an event in time: first closure, then pressure or nasal airflow, then release.

paragraphs.text: The fricatives and stops fit together into one table built on three properties: **manner of articulation, place of articulation,** and **voice.** Manner of articulation is how the air is shaped, whether through a narrow gap as in a fricative, a full closure with the nose sealed as in an oral stop, or a full closure with the nose open as in a nasal stop.

paragraphs.text: The places run from the front of the mouth to the back: **labial, dental, alveolar, postalveolar,** and **velar.**

paragraphs.text: The fricatives fill the labial, dental, alveolar, and postalveolar columns, each with a voiceless and voiced member: f and v, th and th, s and z, and sh and j.

paragraphs.text: The oral stops fill the labial, alveolar, and velar columns: voiceless p, t, and k, and voiced b, d, and g.

paragraphs.text: The nasal stops fill the same three columns as the oral stops, and all of them are voiced: m, n, and ng.

paragraphs.text: Every one of these consonants can be described by a combination of three values. For example, t is a **voiceless alveolar oral stop,** and z is a **voiced alveolar fricative.** Changing just one value produces a different sound: changing t from voiceless to voiced gives d, and changing d from an oral stop to a nasal stop gives n.

paragraphs.text: The empty cells are also informative. None of these English consonants is a dental or postalveolar stop, and none is a velar fricative. The sounds of English are therefore not a random collection of noises but a **highly structured system** of shared properties.

paragraphs.text: Every English speaker already uses this system every time they talk, without ever having been taught the table. This means a speaker's knowledge of English contains a great deal of hidden structure, organized along place, manner, and voice.

paragraphs.text: **Artificial intelligence (AI)** is a model of several **psychological skills that animals have.** The five skills are **knowing, recognizing, attending, acting,** and **learning.**
paragraphs.plain: Artificial intelligence (AI) is a model of several psychological skills that animals have. The five skills are knowing, recognizing, attending, acting, and learning.

paragraphs.text: Knowing is having information stored in a usable form.
paragraphs.plain: Knowing is having information stored in a usable form.

paragraphs.text: Recognizing is identifying something from the input that arrives.
paragraphs.plain: Recognizing is identifying something from the input that arrives.

paragraphs.text: Attending is selecting which parts of the input to focus on.
paragraphs.plain: Attending is selecting which parts of the input to focus on.

paragraphs.text: Acting is producing a behavior or output.
paragraphs.plain: Acting is producing a behavior or output.

paragraphs.text: Learning is changing over time based on experience.
paragraphs.plain: Learning is changing over time based on experience.

paragraphs.text: The way AI models each of these skills is **at least slightly based on how humans perform them.** This goes against a common view that AI is purely a technical innovation that appeared out of nowhere. AI grew out of ideas about human and animal psychology, and each part of an AI system can be traced back to a human skill it was built to imitate.

AI grew out of ideas about human and animal psychology, and each part of an AI system can be traced back to a human skill it was built to imitate.

paragraphs.text: The question of how AI **knows** something connects to a 1953 paper by **Wilson** L. **Taylor** titled **"Cloze Procedure": A New Tool for Measuring Readability.** It was published in the Fall 1953 issue of **Journalism Quarterly,** a journal devoted to research studies in the field of mass communications.

It was published in the Fall 1953 issue of Journalism Quarterly, a journal devoted to research studies in the field of mass communications.

paragraphs.text: The paper was the first comprehensive statement of a research method and its theory, which had been introduced briefly during a workshop at the 1953 **AEJ convention.**

paragraphs.text: It reported findings from **three pilot studies and two experiments** in which cloze procedure results were compared with the results of two existing **readability formulas,** which are formulas that estimate how easy a piece of writing is to read.

paragraphs.text: At the center of Taylor's method is a unit of measurement called a **cloze.** It is pronounced like the verb "close," and the name comes from the word **closure.**

paragraphs.text: **Closure** is a term from **Gestalt psychology,** the branch of psychology that studies how we perceive whole patterns. It refers to the human tendency to **complete a familiar pattern that is not quite finished.**
paragraphs.plain: Closure is a term from Gestalt psychology, the branch of psychology that studies how we perceive whole patterns. It refers to the human tendency to complete a familiar pattern that is not quite finished.

paragraphs.text: The standard example is a broken circle. We tend to see a circle with a gap as a whole circle, filling in the missing piece in our minds.

paragraphs.text: Given the sentence "Chickens cackle and ___ quack," almost anyone can instantly supply the word "ducks."

paragraphs.text: Filling that single blank requires a surprising amount of knowledge. The sentence is a complex pattern built out of many smaller patterns.

paragraphs.text: Beyond single words, a reader must know the meanings of **combinations** of words.

paragraphs.text: The reader must also notice that the sentence is built in two parallel halves. The first half pairs an animal with its sound, "chickens cackle," so the second half calls for the animal that goes with the sound "quack."

paragraphs.text: In other words, a reader has to guess what the incomplete sentence means as a whole and then complete its pattern to fit that whole meaning.

paragraphs.text: Taylor gave two formal definitions.

paragraphs.text: A **cloze unit** is any single occurrence of a **successful attempt to reproduce accurately a part deleted from a "message",** where a message is any language product, by deciding from the context that remains what the missing part should be.

paragraphs.text: **Cloze procedure** is a method of **intercepting a message from a "transmitter",** which is a writer or speaker, **mutilating its language patterns by deleting parts,** and giving the damaged message to **"receivers",** who are readers or listeners. The receivers' attempts to make the patterns whole again produce a large number of cloze units, which can be counted.

The receivers' attempts to make the patterns whole again produce a large number of cloze units, which can be counted.

paragraphs.text: AI shows that it knows something by **demonstrating the ability to complete, or cloze, sequences.** A system that can reliably fill in the missing parts of language has captured the patterns of that language.

paragraphs.text: The same kind of test works for people. A teacher can test a student's knowledge of a skill by asking the student to complete some sequence, such as finishing a sentence, supplying the next step in a procedure, or filling in a missing word. Success at completion is taken as evidence of knowledge.

paragraphs.text: AI takes this idea to its limit. From the AI point of view, **knowledge is nothing more than completion.** A system counts as knowing English if, given part of an English sequence, it can correctly produce what comes next or what is missing, and no further ingredient beyond that ability is required.

paragraphs.text: **GPT** is a system that takes in a sequence of words and predicts what word should come next. The words themselves are the input, so the first question is what a word looks like to a computer.

paragraphs.text: To a computer, a word is simply **a bunch of random numbers.** Each word in the vocabulary is assigned its own set of numbers, and the only strict requirement at the start is that **no two words share the same set of numbers.** The numbers do not need to mean anything at first, as long as each word can be told apart from every other word.

sections.title: How GPT Transforms Inputs into Predictions

paragraphs.text: The list of probabilities that GPT produces is called a **pdf,** short for **probability distribution function.** It describes how likely each possible next word is. The input vectors are labeled the **x's,** so the central question is how the system turns the x's into the pdf.

paragraphs.text: GPT transforms the inputs **through recognizing by computing.** It recognizes the pattern in the input words, and that recognition is carried out entirely through computation.

sections.title: The Octopus as a Dynamical System

paragraphs.text: An octopus defending its den is a clear example of a dynamical system in behavior. Its **elements** are its 8 **arms** and the **ground** it is sitting on and pushing against.

paragraphs.text: The **relations** in this system are the coordinated connections between each individual arm, the ground, and the fish the octopus is interacting with. These relations are **planned by a neural system** that lives in the octopus's head and also throughout the rest of its body. The octopus does not control its arms from one central point alone; the planning is spread across the body.

paragraphs.text: Human speech is also a dynamical system, and it has many more elements than the octopus example. The **elements** are the **many parts of the tongue,** the **lips,** the **velum,** the **larynx,** the **palate,** and the **pharyngeal wall.**

paragraphs.text: There are so many dynamical systems in nature that we can **use one dynamical system to study another.** Two systems can be extremely different on the surface, such as an octopus arm and a human tongue, while still sharing an **underlying similarity** in how their elements, relations, and goals are organized.

sections.title: AI as a Model of Animal Psychological Skills

paragraphs.text: **AI** is a **model of several animal psychological skills.** It is a system built to imitate abilities that animals, including humans, already have. The five skills are **knowing, recognizing, attending, acting,** and **learning.**
paragraphs.plain: AI is a model of several animal psychological skills. It is a system built to imitate abilities that animals, including humans, already have. The five skills are knowing, recognizing, attending, acting, and learning.

paragraphs.text: **Knowing** is holding stored information about the world, such as information about how words are used.
paragraphs.plain: Knowing is holding stored information about the world, such as information about how words are used.

paragraphs.text: **Recognizing** is identifying what something is when it is encountered, such as recognizing a word or a face.
paragraphs.plain: Recognizing is identifying what something is when it is encountered, such as recognizing a word or a face.

paragraphs.text: **Attending** is focusing on the parts of the input that matter most at a given moment.
paragraphs.plain: Attending is focusing on the parts of the input that matter most at a given moment.

paragraphs.text: **Acting** is producing an output, such as a movement for an animal or a word for a language model.
paragraphs.plain: Acting is producing an output, such as a movement for an animal or a word for a language model.

paragraphs.text: **Learning** is changing internal knowledge based on experience so that future performance improves.
paragraphs.plain: Learning is changing internal knowledge based on experience so that future performance improves.

paragraphs.text: The **Cloze Procedure** is an early example of measuring one of these skills in humans. It was introduced by **Wilson** L. **Taylor** in **"'Cloze Procedure': A New Tool for Measuring Readability,"** published in **Journalism Quarterly** in **Fall 1953.**

sections.title: How GPT Predicts the Next Word

paragraphs.text: In GPT, each word is represented as a **vector,** which is a list of **thousands of numbers.** We call these vectors **x's** or **tokens.** In the example sentence **"chickens cackle and ducks,"** each of the four words is its own tall column of numbers, one column for each token.

paragraphs.text: All of the AI's **knowledge** about speech, language, or anything else is stored in **a few trillion numbers** called **weights,** or **w's.** The weights are not a dictionary or a list of facts; they are numbers whose values together determine how the system responds to input.

paragraphs.text: The AI combines its knowledge, the **W's,** with the input vectors, the **x's,** using mostly the four basic operations: **addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division (+ ,−,× ,÷).** The complexity of the system comes from the enormous number of these simple calculations, not from any complicated single operation.

The complexity of the system comes from the enormous number of these simple calculations, not from any complicated single operation.

paragraphs.text: These calculations produce a **probability distribution function** over possible next words. A **probability distribution** assigns each possible word a probability, and all the probabilities together add up to one. This distribution is the system's way of saying, "this is my guess for the next word."

paragraphs.text: Training follows a repeated sequence of steps:

paragraphs.text: 1. The system **starts with random W's.** These are completely random numbers, and any values at all can be used as the starting point.

paragraphs.text: 2. The system is given a sequence of words, such as **"chickens cackle and ducks,"** and is asked to **predict the next word** by combining its W's with the input vectors.

paragraphs.text: 3. With random weights, the prediction is poor. The system's distribution might have its tallest peak over **"cat,"** with only low, uneven probability spread across the other words, including "quack."

paragraphs.text: 4. We already know the correct next word is **"quack."** The **target distribution** puts all of the probability on "quack" as a single sharp spike and zero probability on every other word. We tell the system to **change its W's** so that its output distribution looks more like this target.

paragraphs.text: 5. The system is exposed to **more sequences** and asked to predict the next word again, **billions of times,** and each time its W's are changed to **improve its guessing.**

paragraphs.text: This repeated cycle of guessing, comparing to the correct answer, and adjusting the weights is **how** LLMs **learn and know.** An LLM, or **large language model,** gets all of its knowledge from this process of gradually correcting random weights over billions of examples.

paragraphs.text: AI learning depends on **two tricks,** each captured by a phrase in an image generated by **ChatGPT.**

paragraphs.text: The first trick is **"Fake It Till You Make It."** The system begins with **random weights** and makes predictions right away, even though those first predictions are essentially meaningless. It does not wait until it has knowledge before acting; it acts first and gains knowledge along the way.

paragraphs.text: The second trick is **"Learn by Making Mistakes."** Each wrong prediction produces an **error,** which is the difference between what the system guessed and what was correct. The system uses that error to adjust its weights, so every mistake becomes information that improves the next prediction.

sections.title: Propagating Values Backward with Bellman's Rule

paragraphs.text: The bigger problems are solved by **propagating Values** from each stage to the earlier stage using Bellman's idea. To propagate means to pass information along, and here the information moves from later stages to earlier ones.

paragraphs.text: **Bellman's rule** states that the Value at one state is the minimum of a set of numbers. Each number in the set is the sum of the cost to one of the next states and the Value at that next state. Every equation from VAJ down to VDJ ,VEJ, and VFJ follows this same pattern.

sections.title: The Elements of the Harmonic Oscillator, x and v

paragraphs.text: A **harmonic oscillator** is built from only two quantities, x and v. We can think of x as how far something is displaced from its resting point, and v as its **velocity,** which is how fast and in which direction x is moving. Neither variable is interesting alone. The whole system is about **how x and v change over time as a result of their relation to each other.**
paragraphs.plain: A harmonic oscillator is built from only two quantities, x and v. We can think of x as how far something is displaced from its resting point, and v as its velocity, which is how fast and in which direction x is moving. Neither variable is interesting alone. The whole system is about how x and v change over time as a result of their relation to each other.

paragraphs.text: To talk about change over time, we put a dot over a variable. ẋ means the change in x as time increases, and v̇ means the change in v as time increases. This way of writing rates of change is **Isaac Newton's notation.**
paragraphs.plain: To talk about change over time, we put a dot over a variable. ẋ means the change in x as time increases, and v̇ means the change in v as time increases. This way of writing rates of change is Isaac Newton's notation.

paragraphs.text: The sign of the dotted quantity tells us the direction of change. When ẋ is positive, x is rising, and when ẋ is negative, x is falling.
paragraphs.plain: The sign of the dotted quantity tells us the direction of change. When ẋ is positive, x is rising, and when ẋ is negative, x is falling.

paragraphs.text: The same rule holds for v. A positive v̇ means v is rising, and a negative v̇ means v is falling.
paragraphs.plain: The same rule holds for v. A positive v̇ means v is rising, and a negative v̇ means v is falling.

paragraphs.text: The size of the dotted quantity tells us how quickly the change happens. A large positive ẋ means x is climbing quickly, and a small positive ẋ means it is climbing slowly.
paragraphs.plain: The size of the dotted quantity tells us how quickly the change happens. A large positive ẋ means x is climbing quickly, and a small positive ẋ means it is climbing slowly.

paragraphs.text: The defining feature of the harmonic oscillator is that x **and v change each other.** The rate at which x changes is set by v, and the rate at which v changes is set by x. Neither variable can change on its own terms, and this two-way dependence is what produces repeating back-and-forth motion.
paragraphs.plain: The defining feature of the harmonic oscillator is that x and v change each other. The rate at which x changes is set by v, and the rate at which v changes is set by x. Neither variable can change on its own terms, and this two-way dependence is what produces repeating back-and-forth motion.

sections.title: The Two Equations of the Harmonic Oscillator

paragraphs.text: The first equation says that the rate of change of x equals the current value of v:
paragraphs.plain: The first equation says that the rate of change of x equals the current value of v:

paragraphs.text: ẋ = v
paragraphs.plain: ẋ = v

paragraphs.text: When v is positive, ẋ is positive, so x rises.
paragraphs.plain: When v is positive, ẋ is positive, so x rises.

paragraphs.text: When v is negative, ẋ is negative, so x falls.
paragraphs.plain: When v is negative, ẋ is negative, so x falls.

paragraphs.text: In other words, v directly steers x. Whatever sign v has at a given moment is the direction x moves at that moment.
paragraphs.plain: In other words, v directly steers x. Whatever sign v has at a given moment is the direction x moves at that moment.

paragraphs.text: The second equation says that the rate of change of v equals the negative of x:
paragraphs.plain: The second equation says that the rate of change of v equals the negative of x:

paragraphs.text: v̇ = −x
paragraphs.plain: v̇ = −x

paragraphs.text: The **minus sign** is the heart of the system. It means v is always pushed in the direction opposite to wherever x currently is.
paragraphs.plain: The minus sign is the heart of the system. It means v is always pushed in the direction opposite to wherever x currently is.

paragraphs.text: When x is positive, v̇ is negative, so v falls. As v keeps falling, it eventually becomes negative, and through the first equation that negative v makes x fall back down.
paragraphs.plain: When x is positive, v̇ is negative, so v falls. As v keeps falling, it eventually becomes negative, and through the first equation that negative v makes x fall back down.

paragraphs.text: When x is negative, v̇ is positive, so v rises. Once v becomes positive, the first equation makes x rise back up.
paragraphs.plain: When x is negative, v̇ is positive, so v rises. Once v becomes positive, the first equation makes x rise back up.

paragraphs.text: Putting the two equations together, whenever x moves away from zero in either direction, the second equation turns v around, and the first equation then carries x back toward zero. This **restoring relationship** is what keeps the system from drifting off and instead makes it swing back and forth.
paragraphs.plain: Putting the two equations together, whenever x moves away from zero in either direction, the second equation turns v around, and the first equation then carries x back toward zero. This restoring relationship is what keeps the system from drifting off and instead makes it swing back and forth.

paragraphs.text: The relationship can be drawn as a **loop of influence** with x and v each in a circle. One arrow runs from v to x, standing for ẋ = v, since v determines how x changes. A second arrow runs from x back to v, standing for v̇ = −x, since x determines how v changes.
paragraphs.plain: The relationship can be drawn as a loop of influence with x and v each in a circle. One arrow runs from v to x, standing for ẋ = v, since v determines how x changes. A second arrow runs from x back to v, standing for v̇ = −x, since x determines how v changes.

paragraphs.text: The loop is closed, so a change in v changes x, and that change in x goes on to change v again.
paragraphs.plain: The loop is closed, so a change in v changes x, and that change in x goes on to change v again.

paragraphs.text: The same two-variable structure of ẋ = v and v̇ = −x shows up in a huge range of systems, including the air in the vocal tract, the vocal folds, economies, music, and matter itself.

The harmonic oscillator is still useful as a model, since it captures the basic back-and-forth pattern that all of these systems share.

sections.title: A Slice of Air in the Vocal Tract

paragraphs.text: The **vocal tract** is the air-filled passage from the vocal folds in the throat up through the mouth to the lips. We can picture a thin slice of air inside it, containing a large number of air particles.
paragraphs.plain: The vocal tract is the air-filled passage from the vocal folds in the throat up through the mouth to the lips. We can picture a thin slice of air inside it, containing a large number of air particles.

paragraphs.text: **Pressure** in this slice depends on how close together the particles are.
paragraphs.plain: Pressure in this slice depends on how close together the particles are.

paragraphs.text: **High pressure** means the air particles are very close together.
paragraphs.plain: High pressure means the air particles are very close together.

paragraphs.text: **Low pressure** means the air particles are very far apart.

paragraphs.text: The particles themselves stay the same. There are the same number of them, and each one is the same size. The only thing that changes is the distance between them.

paragraphs.text: **Compression** is the state in which particles are squeezed closer together than their normal spacing. **Rarefaction** is the state in which particles are spread farther apart than their normal spacing. The normal spacing, where the air is neither squeezed nor stretched, is the **equilibrium spacing.**

paragraphs.text: If we track one pair of neighboring particles, at equilibrium they sit at 100% of their equilibrium distance.

paragraphs.text: At the strongest compression, that pair is squeezed to about 56% of its equilibrium distance, so the particles are a little more than half as far apart as usual.

paragraphs.text: The slice cycles continuously between these states. It compresses, passes back through equilibrium, rarefies, and passes back through equilibrium again. In real speech the motion is much smaller than these exaggerated values, and the slice is an idealized piece of the air.

Air that is squeezed together tends to push itself apart, and air that is spread out tends to be pulled back together, so any departure from equilibrium spacing is pushed back toward equilibrium. sections.title: Vowels and the Shape of the Vocal Tract

paragraphs.text: Vowels differ from one another in where the **tongue** sits inside the vocal tract. These positions can be imaged with magnetic resonance imaging, which produces a picture of the head cut down the middle from front to back, showing the lips, tongue, roof of the mouth, and throat. In these images the speaker faces left, the tongue is the large bright mass in the mouth, and the dark regions are air.

These positions can be imaged with magnetic resonance imaging, which produces a picture of the head cut down the middle from front to back, showing the lips, tongue, roof of the mouth, and throat. In these images the speaker faces left, the tongue is the large bright mass in the mouth, and the dark regions are air.

paragraphs.text: Vowels are organized along two dimensions. **Height** describes whether the tongue body is raised toward the roof of the mouth **(high)** or lowered **(low). Frontness** describes whether the tongue body is pushed forward toward the teeth **(front),** pulled back toward the throat **(back),** or held in between **(central).**

Frontness describes whether the tongue body is pushed forward toward the teeth (front), pulled back toward the throat (back), or held in between (central).

paragraphs.text: In **"dean,"** the vowel is **high and front.** The tongue body is raised and pushed forward, close to the hard roof of the mouth, which leaves a large open air space in the throat behind the tongue.
paragraphs.plain: In "dean," the vowel is high and front. The tongue body is raised and pushed forward, close to the hard roof of the mouth, which leaves a large open air space in the throat behind the tongue.

paragraphs.text: In **"dune,"** the vowel is **high and back.** The tongue is still raised, but its highest point is pulled back toward the soft rear part of the roof of the mouth.

paragraphs.text: In **"Dan,"** the vowel is **low and front.** The tongue is lowered and the mouth is more open, with the tongue body still positioned toward the front.
paragraphs.plain: In "Dan," the vowel is low and front. The tongue is lowered and the mouth is more open, with the tongue body still positioned toward the front.

paragraphs.text: In **"Don,"** the vowel is **low and back.** The tongue is lowered and pulled back into the throat, which narrows the air space behind it.
paragraphs.plain: In "Don," the vowel is low and back. The tongue is lowered and pulled back into the throat, which narrows the air space behind it.

paragraphs.text: In **"done,"** the vowel is **central.** The tongue rests in the middle of the mouth, neither strongly raised nor lowered and neither pushed forward nor pulled back.

paragraphs.text: Each tongue position gives the air in the vocal tract a different shape. A differently shaped column of air vibrates in a different way, and that difference in vibration is what makes one vowel sound different from another.
paragraphs.plain: Each tongue position gives the air in the vocal tract a different shape. A differently shaped column of air vibrates in a different way, and that difference in vibration is what makes one vowel sound different from another.

paragraphs.text: A single cosine describes air vibrating at one frequency. A vowel is more complex than that. The air in the vocal tract vibrates at **several frequencies at the same time,** and the vowel is the **sum** of those vibrations. Since each individual vibration is a cosine, and each cosine is the behavior of a harmonic oscillator, a vowel can be modeled as **harmonic oscillators added together.**

Since each individual vibration is a cosine, and each cosine is the behavior of a harmonic oscillator, a vowel can be modeled as harmonic oscillators added together.

paragraphs.text: **Frequency** is the number of complete cycles a vibration makes per second, measured in **hertz (Hz).** A vibration at f hertz can be written as cos(2πft), where t is time in seconds. Multiplying by 2π converts the number of cycles into phase, since one full cycle equals a phase of 2π.

paragraphs.text: The vowel **/i/,** the vowel in "dean," is modeled as a combination of a 1 Hz vibration and a 4 Hz vibration:

sections.title: Two Things Are Vibrating, the Vocal Tract Air and the Vocal Folds

paragraphs.text: During speech, **two things vibrate.** The first is the air in the vocal tract, which is the vibration modeled by the cosines and sums of cosines above. The second is the **vocal folds.**
paragraphs.plain: During speech, two things vibrate. The first is the air in the vocal tract, which is the vibration modeled by the cosines and sums of cosines above. The second is the vocal folds.

paragraphs.text: The vocal folds are two folds of tissue in the **larynx,** the voice box in the throat. When air from the lungs pushes up against the closed folds, pressure builds until the folds are forced apart. Once they open and air rushes through, the pressure between them drops and the folds come back together. The cycle then repeats many times per second.
paragraphs.plain: The vocal folds are two folds of tissue in the larynx, the voice box in the throat. When air from the lungs pushes up against the closed folds, pressure builds until the folds are forced apart. Once they open and air rushes through, the pressure between them drops and the folds come back together. The cycle then repeats many times per second.

paragraphs.text: This repeated opening and closing is itself an oscillation, with the folds swinging away from their closed position and being pulled back again.
paragraphs.plain: This repeated opening and closing is itself an oscillation, with the folds swinging away from their closed position and being pulled back again.

paragraphs.text: Each opening lets a puff of air through, so the vocal folds chop the steady airflow from the lungs into a rapid series of puffs.
paragraphs.plain: Each opening lets a puff of air through, so the vocal folds chop the steady airflow from the lungs into a rapid series of puffs.

paragraphs.text: Those puffs set the air in the vocal tract vibrating, and the shape of the vocal tract, set by the tongue position, determines which combination of frequencies that air vibrates at.
paragraphs.plain: Those puffs set the air in the vocal tract vibrating, and the shape of the vocal tract, set by the tongue position, determines which combination of frequencies that air vibrates at.

paragraphs.text: Speech sounds such as vowels therefore come from one oscillator driving another. The vocal folds vibrate, and the air in the vocal tract vibrates in response.
