sections.title: Matter and the Quantum Harmonic Oscillator

paragraphs.text: The harmonic oscillator appears in physics at the scale of atoms as the **quantum harmonic oscillator.** In quantum physics, a vibrating system cannot vibrate with just any amount of energy. It can only take certain specific energy levels, which is what **quantized** means.
paragraphs.plain: The harmonic oscillator appears in physics at the scale of atoms as the quantum harmonic oscillator. In quantum physics, a vibrating system cannot vibrate with just any amount of energy. It can only take certain specific energy levels, which is what quantized means.

paragraphs.text: **Matter is made up of atoms with different numbers of electrons, some vibrating at a low frequency and some at a high frequency.** In the quantum description, electrons in an atom are not tiny balls on tracks but **wave modes,** which are specific allowed patterns of vibration.
paragraphs.plain: Matter is made up of atoms with different numbers of electrons, some vibrating at a low frequency and some at a high frequency. In the quantum description, electrons in an atom are not tiny balls on tracks but wave modes, which are specific allowed patterns of vibration.

paragraphs.text: **Magnesium** (Mg) shows two ways of picturing an atom. A neutral magnesium atom has 12 **electrons,** and its nucleus contains 12 **protons.** Its **ground-state configuration,** the arrangement of electrons at lowest energy, is written 1s² 2s² 2p⁶ 3s² .

paragraphs.text: In the older **"solar system" picture,** also called the **Bohr-style shell** picture, electrons are drawn as particles moving on circular paths around the nucleus. Magnesium's electrons are arranged in shells of 2, 8, **and 2: 2** electrons in shell 1, 8 electrons in shell 2, and 2 electrons in shell 3. This is a historical model of how the shells are arranged.

sections.title: A Slice of Air in the Vocal Tract

paragraphs.text: The air inside the vocal tract can be treated as a small slice of material made of many particles. During speech, the particles in the slice stay the same, and each particle stays the same size. **What changes is the distance between the particles.**

paragraphs.text: **Damping** is the gradual loss of motion over time, which comes from the viscous, frictional part of the spring. In a lightly damped system, the damping is small, so each swing is only a little smaller than the one before it and the oscillation continues for many cycles.

paragraphs.text: **Perturbation theory** is the study of how a system's behavior changes when one of its parameters is nudged up or down. A **parameter** is a fixed setting of a system, such as how heavy the mass is or how stiff the spring is. For a mass-spring system, the behavior of interest is its **frequency,** meaning how many oscillations it completes per second.
paragraphs.plain: Perturbation theory is the study of how a system's behavior changes when one of its parameters is nudged up or down. A parameter is a fixed setting of a system, such as how heavy the mass is or how stiff the spring is. For a mass-spring system, the behavior of interest is its frequency, meaning how many oscillations it completes per second.

paragraphs.text: **If we increase the mass m of a mass-spring system, the frequency decreases.**
paragraphs.plain: If we increase the mass m of a mass-spring system, the frequency decreases.

paragraphs.text: A heavier mass carries its motion more strongly, so the spring takes longer to slow it down and turn it around at each end of its swing.
paragraphs.plain: A heavier mass carries its motion more strongly, so the spring takes longer to slow it down and turn it around at each end of its swing.

paragraphs.text: Each cycle therefore takes longer, and fewer cycles fit into each second. **More mass means a lower frequency.**
paragraphs.plain: Each cycle therefore takes longer, and fewer cycles fit into each second. More mass means a lower frequency.

paragraphs.text: **If we increase the stiffness k of the spring, the frequency increases.**
paragraphs.plain: If we increase the stiffness k of the spring, the frequency increases.

paragraphs.text: A stiffer spring pulls back harder on the mass for the same displacement, so it turns the mass around more quickly at each end of its swing.
paragraphs.plain: A stiffer spring pulls back harder on the mass for the same displacement, so it turns the mass around more quickly at each end of its swing.

paragraphs.text: Each cycle therefore takes less time, and more cycles fit into each second. **More stiffness means a higher frequency.**
paragraphs.plain: Each cycle therefore takes less time, and more cycles fit into each second. More stiffness means a higher frequency.

paragraphs.text: These two results together form the core perturbation-theory relationships for a mass- spring system:
paragraphs.plain: These two results together form the core perturbation-theory relationships for a mass- spring system:

paragraphs.text: **Increasing mass lowers frequency.**
paragraphs.plain: Increasing mass lowers frequency.

paragraphs.text: **Increasing stiffness raises frequency.**
paragraphs.plain: Increasing stiffness raises frequency.

paragraphs.text: These relationships give us a way to predict how a vibrating system will sound or behave just from knowing whether it is heavy or light and stiff or loose.
paragraphs.plain: These relationships give us a way to predict how a vibrating system will sound or behave just from knowing whether it is heavy or light and stiff or loose.

paragraphs.text: The mass-spring relationships explain how the ear separates sounds by frequency. This explanation comes from the work of **Georg von Békésy,** who received the **Nobel Prize in** 1961 for discovering how the inner ear responds to sound.

paragraphs.text: Inside the inner ear is a long, tapered membrane called the **basilar membrane.** It is wide at one end and narrow at the other, and its physical properties change gradually along its length.
paragraphs.plain: Inside the inner ear is a long, tapered membrane called the basilar membrane. It is wide at one end and narrow at the other, and its physical properties change gradually along its length.

paragraphs.text: At the **wide end,** the membrane has **large mass M** and **small stiffness k.** It is heavy and loose.
paragraphs.plain: At the wide end, the membrane has large mass M and small stiffness k. It is heavy and loose.

paragraphs.text: At the **narrow end,** the membrane has **small mass m** and **large stiffness K.** It is light and stiff.
paragraphs.plain: At the narrow end, the membrane has small mass m and large stiffness K. It is light and stiff.

paragraphs.text: Moving along the membrane from the wide end to the narrow end, mass steadily decreases and stiffness steadily increases.
paragraphs.plain: Moving along the membrane from the wide end to the narrow end, mass steadily decreases and stiffness steadily increases.

paragraphs.text: Applying perturbation theory to each location on the membrane gives each location its own preferred frequency.
paragraphs.plain: Applying perturbation theory to each location on the membrane gives each location its own preferred frequency.

paragraphs.text: At the wide end, large mass lowers the frequency and small stiffness also lowers the frequency. This end vibrates most strongly for **low-frequency** sounds.

paragraphs.text: At the narrow end, small mass raises the frequency and large stiffness also raises the frequency. This end vibrates most strongly for **high-frequency** sounds.

paragraphs.text: Every point in between has an intermediate mass and stiffness, so every point is tuned to an intermediate frequency. The membrane is effectively a long row of mass-spring systems, each set to a slightly different frequency.

paragraphs.text: **Nerve fibers** leave the membrane at many different locations along its length. When a particular spot on the membrane vibrates, the fibers at that spot become active, and which fibers are active tells the brain which frequencies are present in the sound.

paragraphs.text: When a vowel made of two combined frequencies reaches the ear, such as the 1 Hz and 4 Hz combination for /i/, two different places along the membrane vibrate, one for each frequency. The membrane separates the combined vibration back into its component frequencies.

paragraphs.text: In machine learning, a model is trained by repeatedly updating a value to move it toward a target. The **learning rate,** written γ, sets how large each update is, as a fraction of the remaining distance to the target. Each full round of updates through the training data is called an **epoch.**
paragraphs.plain: In machine learning, a model is trained by repeatedly updating a value to move it toward a target. The learning rate, written γ, sets how large each update is, as a fraction of the remaining distance to the target. Each full round of updates through the training data is called an epoch.

paragraphs.text: The effect of γ can be seen by training three runs that start at very different values, one near 130, one near 80, and one near 10, and all head toward a target of about 80. Each run is tracked over 300 epochs at four different learning rates.

paragraphs.text: At a **learning rate of 1%,** the runs move smoothly and slowly. The run starting at 130 curves down gradually and is still at about 82 after 300 epochs. The run starting at 10 curves up gradually and has only reached about 76 after 300 epochs. The motion is very steady, but the runs have not fully reached the target even by the end.

The run starting at 10 curves up gradually and has only reached about 76 after 300 epochs. The motion is very steady, but the runs have not fully reached the target even by the end.

paragraphs.text: At a **learning rate of 10%,** the runs reach the neighborhood of 80 within roughly the first 30 to 50 epochs. After arriving, they stay close to 80 with small wiggles of a few units above and below.

paragraphs.text: At a **learning rate of 50%,** the runs jump to the region of 80 within just a few epochs. After that, they bounce around noisily, swinging roughly between 70 and 95 rather than sitting on the target.

paragraphs.text: At a **learning rate of 80%,** the runs reach the target region almost immediately, but they bounce even more widely, roughly between 68 and 97, for all 300 epochs.

paragraphs.text: These results show the **fundamental learning tradeoff:**
paragraphs.plain: These results show the fundamental learning tradeoff:

paragraphs.text: **When γ increases, speed increases and accuracy decreases.** Large updates get the value to the target region quickly, but the same large updates keep throwing the value past the target, so it oscillates around the answer instead of settling on it.
paragraphs.plain: When γ increases, speed increases and accuracy decreases. Large updates get the value to the target region quickly, but the same large updates keep throwing the value past the target, so it oscillates around the answer instead of settling on it.

paragraphs.text: **When γ decreases, speed decreases and accuracy increases.** Small updates keep the value on a smooth, steady path with very little bouncing, but they take many more epochs to arrive.

paragraphs.text: This is the **oscillation in** SGD that appears among the everyday examples of vibration. A high learning rate turns training into a back-and-forth swinging motion around the target.

paragraphs.text: The tradeoff is an unfortunate one, since in practice we want both fast learning and accurate learning at the same time. **Thousands of people, over generations, have made their living by finding better ways to optimize,** meaning better training methods that raise both speed and accuracy together rather than trading one against the other.

paragraphs.text: **A spring stops at a place, but a mass stops after a process.** This single idea separates two very different kinds of motion. A spring with no mass attached returns to one location and stays there. A spring with a mass attached keeps moving past that location, back and forth, before it finally comes to rest.
paragraphs.plain: A spring stops at a place, but a mass stops after a process. This single idea separates two very different kinds of motion. A spring with no mass attached returns to one location and stays there. A spring with a mass attached keeps moving past that location, back and forth, before it finally comes to rest.

paragraphs.text: Everything here is measured with one number, the **displacement x.** Displacement is how far the end of the spring is from its **natural position,** the place where the spring rests when nothing is pulling or pushing on it. We call the natural position x = 0, a stretch to the right x = +1, and a squeeze to the left x = −1.
paragraphs.plain: Everything here is measured with one number, the displacement x. Displacement is how far the end of the spring is from its natural position, the place where the spring rests when nothing is pulling or pushing on it. We call the natural position x = 0, a stretch to the right x = +1, and a squeeze to the left x = −1.

paragraphs.text: **The spring alone, pulled out.** Picture a spring fixed to a wall at one end, lying on a table, with nothing attached to its free end. If we pull the free end out to x = +1 and let go, the spring pulls itself back and stops exactly at x = 0. It does not overshoot.
paragraphs.plain: The spring alone, pulled out. Picture a spring fixed to a wall at one end, lying on a table, with nothing attached to its free end. If we pull the free end out to x = +1 and let go, the spring pulls itself back and stops exactly at x = 0. It does not overshoot.

paragraphs.text: When we plot x against time for this release, the curve starts at +1 and bends downward, dropping quickly at first and then more and more slowly. The curve gets closer and closer to 0 but never crosses below it. The label for this motion is **"x approaches 0 without crossing it."**
paragraphs.plain: When we plot x against time for this release, the curve starts at +1 and bends downward, dropping quickly at first and then more and more slowly. The curve gets closer and closer to 0 but never crosses below it. The label for this motion is "x approaches 0 without crossing it."

paragraphs.text: The reason the motion slows down is that the pull of the spring depends on how far it is stretched. A large stretch produces a large pull back, and a small stretch produces a small pull. As the end gets close to x = 0, the pull becomes almost zero, so the motion becomes almost zero too.
paragraphs.plain: The reason the motion slows down is that the pull of the spring depends on how far it is stretched. A large stretch produces a large pull back, and a small stretch produces a small pull. As the end gets close to x = 0, the pull becomes almost zero, so the motion becomes almost zero too.

paragraphs.text: **The spring alone, pushed in.** The same thing happens in the opposite direction. If we squeeze the spring to x = −1 and release it, the spring pushes itself back out and settles at x = 0.
paragraphs.plain: The spring alone, pushed in. The same thing happens in the opposite direction. If we squeeze the spring to x = −1 and release it, the spring pushes itself back out and settles at x = 0.

paragraphs.text: Plotted against time, this curve starts at −1 and rises toward 0, again quickly at first and then more slowly. It flattens out right at 0 and never goes above it. The label is **"x rises toward 0 without crossing it."**
paragraphs.plain: Plotted against time, this curve starts at −1 and rises toward 0, again quickly at first and then more slowly. It flattens out right at 0 and never goes above it. The label is "x rises toward 0 without crossing it."

paragraphs.text: Whether we start from +1 or −1, a massless spring always ends at the same place and never passes through it. That is what it means to say a spring **stops at a place.**
paragraphs.plain: Whether we start from +1 or −1, a massless spring always ends at the same place and never passes through it. That is what it means to say a spring stops at a place.

paragraphs.text: **Adding a mass changes the behavior completely.** Now a mass, drawn as a small cart on wheels, is attached to the free end of the spring. We pull the mass to x = +1 and release it. The mass does not stop at x = 0. It shoots right through the natural position and keeps going to the other side.
paragraphs.plain: Adding a mass changes the behavior completely. Now a mass, drawn as a small cart on wheels, is attached to the free end of the spring. We pull the mass to x = +1 and release it. The mass does not stop at x = 0. It shoots right through the natural position and keeps going to the other side.

paragraphs.text: The mass keeps going because a moving mass carries its motion with it. When the mass reaches x = 0, the spring is no longer pulling on it, but the mass is already moving fast, so it continues past 0 and compresses the spring on the other side.
paragraphs.plain: The mass keeps going because a moving mass carries its motion with it. When the mass reaches x = 0, the spring is no longer pulling on it, but the mass is already moving fast, so it continues past 0 and compresses the spring on the other side.

paragraphs.text: Once the spring is compressed, it pushes the mass back. The mass slows down, stops briefly near x = −1, and then gets pushed back through x = 0 toward the positive side again. The label for this is **"the mass carries motion through every crossing."**
paragraphs.plain: Once the spring is compressed, it pushes the mass back. The mass slows down, stops briefly near x = −1, and then gets pushed back through x = 0 toward the positive side again. The label for this is "the mass carries motion through every crossing."

paragraphs.text: Plotted against time, x now makes a wave. It starts at +1, falls through 0 to nearly −1, rises back through 0 to nearly +1, and repeats. This repeating back- and-forth motion is called **oscillation.**
paragraphs.plain: Plotted against time, x now makes a wave. It starts at +1, falls through 0 to nearly −1, rises back through 0 to nearly +1, and repeats. This repeating back- and-forth motion is called oscillation.

paragraphs.text: **Lightly damped oscillation.** Each swing of the mass is slightly smaller than the one before it, so the peaks of the wave shrink a little over time. This is called a **lightly damped oscillation. Damping** is anything that slowly drains away the motion, such as friction. With light damping, the mass swings many times before it finally settles at x = 0.
paragraphs.plain: Lightly damped oscillation. Each swing of the mass is slightly smaller than the one before it, so the peaks of the wave shrink a little over time. This is called a lightly damped oscillation. Damping is anything that slowly drains away the motion, such as friction. With light damping, the mass swings many times before it finally settles at x = 0.

paragraphs.text: This is why a mass **stops after a process.** It does eventually come to rest at the natural position, but only after a long sequence of crossings back and forth, each one a little smaller than the last.
paragraphs.plain: This is why a mass stops after a process. It does eventually come to rest at the natural position, but only after a long sequence of crossings back and forth, each one a little smaller than the last.

paragraphs.text: A mass-spring system therefore has a **frequency,** which is the number of back- and-forth cycles it completes per second. A massless spring has no frequency at all, because it never swings.
paragraphs.plain: A mass-spring system therefore has a frequency, which is the number of back- and-forth cycles it completes per second. A massless spring has no frequency at all, because it never swings.

paragraphs.text: **Perturbation theory** asks what happens to the behavior of a system when we change one of its properties. To **perturb** a system means to nudge one of its settings. For a mass- spring system, the two settings that matter are the **mass m** and the **stiffness k** of the spring, and the behavior we care about is the frequency f of the oscillation.
paragraphs.plain: Perturbation theory asks what happens to the behavior of a system when we change one of its properties. To perturb a system means to nudge one of its settings. For a mass- spring system, the two settings that matter are the mass m and the stiffness k of the spring, and the behavior we care about is the frequency f of the oscillation.

paragraphs.text: **Increasing the mass decreases the frequency.** If we attach a heavier mass to the same spring, it oscillates more slowly, so the frequency goes down.
paragraphs.plain: Increasing the mass decreases the frequency. If we attach a heavier mass to the same spring, it oscillates more slowly, so the frequency goes down.

paragraphs.text: A heavier mass is harder to speed up and harder to slow down. The spring pulls on it with the same strength as before, but that pull changes the heavier mass's speed less. Each swing takes longer, so fewer swings fit into one second.
paragraphs.plain: A heavier mass is harder to speed up and harder to slow down. The spring pulls on it with the same strength as before, but that pull changes the heavier mass's speed less. Each swing takes longer, so fewer swings fit into one second.

paragraphs.text: In short form: when m goes up, f goes down.
paragraphs.plain: In short form: when m goes up, f goes down.

paragraphs.text: **Increasing the stiffness increases the frequency.** If we keep the same mass but use a stiffer spring, the oscillation speeds up, so the frequency goes up.
paragraphs.plain: Increasing the stiffness increases the frequency. If we keep the same mass but use a stiffer spring, the oscillation speeds up, so the frequency goes up.

paragraphs.text: **Stiffness k** is how strongly a spring resists being stretched or squeezed. A stiffer spring pulls back harder for the same amount of stretch. That stronger pull speeds the mass up faster, so each swing finishes sooner and more swings fit into one second.
paragraphs.plain: Stiffness k is how strongly a spring resists being stretched or squeezed. A stiffer spring pulls back harder for the same amount of stretch. That stronger pull speeds the mass up faster, so each swing finishes sooner and more swings fit into one second.

paragraphs.text: In short form: when k goes up, f goes up.
paragraphs.plain: In short form: when k goes up, f goes up.

paragraphs.text: These two rules together are the core of perturbation theory for oscillators. **More mass means lower frequency, and more stiffness means higher frequency.** We do not need to calculate an exact frequency to use these rules. We only need to know which direction the frequency moves when mass or stiffness changes.

We do not need to calculate an exact frequency to use these rules. We only need to know which direction the frequency moves when mass or stiffness changes.

sections.title: Speech as Changing Mass and Stiffness of Air

paragraphs.text: **Speaking changes the effective mass and stiffness of air in the vocal tract.** The **vocal tract** is the air-filled tube running from the vocal folds in the throat up through the mouth to the lips. When we speak, we move the tongue, jaw, and lips, and these movements squeeze some portions of the air in that tube and open up others.
paragraphs.plain: Speaking changes the effective mass and stiffness of air in the vocal tract. The vocal tract is the air-filled tube running from the vocal folds in the throat up through the mouth to the lips. When we speak, we move the tongue, jaw, and lips, and these movements squeeze some portions of the air in that tube and open up others.

paragraphs.text: Squeezing a portion of air in one place changes how much that air acts like a mass and how much it acts like a spring. The **effective mass** and **effective stiffness** of each portion of air are different for every vowel and every consonant, because each sound uses a different shape of the tube.
paragraphs.plain: Squeezing a portion of air in one place changes how much that air acts like a mass and how much it acts like a spring. The effective mass and effective stiffness of each portion of air are different for every vowel and every consonant, because each sound uses a different shape of the tube.

paragraphs.text: The air in the vocal tract is set into vibration by the vibration of the vocal folds. Because the tube has different mass and stiffness in different places, the air vibrates at **many frequencies at once.** The particular set of frequencies depends on **where** the air is squeezed and **how much** it is squeezed, so each vowel and consonant has its own set.

Because the tube has different mass and stiffness in different places, the air vibrates at many frequencies at once. The particular set of frequencies depends on where the air is squeezed and how much it is squeezed, so each vowel and consonant has its own set.

The bright, rounded mass in the middle of each image is the tongue, and the dark regions are the air spaces of the mouth and throat. The five words are **dean, dune, done, Dan, and Don,** which differ only in their vowel.

The brain then has to use that information to decide which sound was spoken.

For a listener to understand speech, the ear has to figure out which low, middle, and high frequencies are present in the speaker's voice and how strong each one is. The brain then has to use that information to decide which sound was spoken.

paragraphs.text: For example, hearing a high frequency of one particular strength together with a low frequency of another particular strength might tell the brain that the word was **"scene."** Hearing two other frequencies instead might tell the brain that the word was **"son."**

paragraphs.text: The question is how the ear separates a single incoming sound into its separate frequencies and reports each one to the brain. The answer lies in the structure of the inner ear.

sections.title: How We Hear and the Cochlea

paragraphs.text: **Sound is a wave of vibration in the air.** When someone speaks, waves of vibration travel through the air and arrive at the listener's **external ear,** the part of the ear on the outside of the head. From there, the vibration travels inward through the ear canal toward the **inner ear.**
paragraphs.plain: Sound is a wave of vibration in the air. When someone speaks, waves of vibration travel through the air and arrive at the listener's external ear, the part of the ear on the outside of the head. From there, the vibration travels inward through the ear canal toward the inner ear.

paragraphs.text: **The cochlea is the part of the inner ear that reports frequencies to the brain.** Of all the structures in the ear, the **cochlea** is the essential one to know by name. It is a small, coiled tube shaped like a snail shell, buried deep inside the bone of the skull. The cochlea is the part that sends signals to the brain saying which frequencies are present in a sound.
paragraphs.plain: The cochlea is the part of the inner ear that reports frequencies to the brain. Of all the structures in the ear, the cochlea is the essential one to know by name. It is a small, coiled tube shaped like a snail shell, buried deep inside the bone of the skull. The cochlea is the part that sends signals to the brain saying which frequencies are present in a sound.

paragraphs.text: **The inner ear and its parts.** In a cutaway view of the head, the outer ear and ear canal lead inward to a tiny structure boxed off deep in the skull, and that boxed region is the inner ear. Enlarged, the inner ear has two main regions.
paragraphs.plain: The inner ear and its parts. In a cutaway view of the head, the outer ear and ear canal lead inward to a tiny structure boxed off deep in the skull, and that boxed region is the inner ear. Enlarged, the inner ear has two main regions.

paragraphs.text: The upper region contains three looping tubes called the **semicircular ducts,** named anterior, lateral, and posterior, along with two small sacs called the **utricle** and **saccule.** Small sensory structures called **cristae** sit inside swellings at the base of the loops, called **ampullae.** These structures are part of the same inner ear but are not the part that separates sound frequencies.

Small sensory structures called cristae sit inside swellings at the base of the loops, called ampullae. These structures are part of the same inner ear but are not the part that separates sound frequencies.

paragraphs.text: The lower region is the coiled **cochlea.** Running through the cochlea are three fluid-filled channels lying side by side: the **vestibular duct,** the **cochlear duct,** and the **tympanic duct.** These channels spiral together around the coil.
paragraphs.plain: The lower region is the coiled cochlea. Running through the cochlea are three fluid-filled channels lying side by side: the vestibular duct, the cochlear duct, and the tympanic duct. These channels spiral together around the coil.

paragraphs.text: The inner ear is built as a set of soft, membrane-walled tubes, called the **membranous labyrinth,** sitting inside a matching set of hollow spaces in hard bone, called the **bony labyrinth.** The soft inner tubes are where the sensing happens, and the bone around them protects them.

paragraphs.text: A bundle of nerve fibers called the **vestibulocochlear nerve** leaves the inner ear and runs toward the brain. This nerve carries the cochlea's signals about sound frequencies to the brain.

paragraphs.text: **Sound reaches the cochlea through a chain of structures.** Sound waves in the air first strike the **tympanic membrane,** which is the eardrum. The tympanic membrane is a thin sheet stretched across the end of the ear canal, and it vibrates back and forth as the air pressure pushes on it.

The tympanic membrane is a thin sheet stretched across the end of the ear canal, and it vibrates back and forth as the air pressure pushes on it.

paragraphs.text: The tympanic membrane is attached to the first of three tiny bones, the **malleus.** When the eardrum vibrates, it moves the malleus.

paragraphs.text: The malleus is connected to the second bone, the **incus,** so the malleus's vibration moves the incus.

paragraphs.text: The incus is connected to the third bone, the **stapes.** The stapes sits against an opening in the cochlea, so when the stapes vibrates, it pushes in and out on the fluid inside the cochlea.

paragraphs.text: **The basilar membrane runs the length of the cochlea.** Inside the coiled cochlea is a long, thin strip of tissue called the **basilar membrane.** It begins near the stapes, where vibration enters the cochlea, and it follows the spiral all the way to the tip of the coil at the center.

paragraphs.text: The opening at the very tip of the coil is called the **helicotrema.** The basilar membrane extends from the stapes end of the cochlea all the way in to the helicotrema.

sections.title: How the Basilar Membrane Separates Frequencies

paragraphs.text: **The basilar membrane is not the same all along its length.** If we imagine uncoiling the cochlea and laying the basilar membrane out flat as a long strip, one end of the strip is wide and the other end is narrow. The wide end is the part near the helicotrema, and the narrow end is the part near the stapes.
paragraphs.plain: The basilar membrane is not the same all along its length. If we imagine uncoiling the cochlea and laying the basilar membrane out flat as a long strip, one end of the strip is wide and the other end is narrow. The wide end is the part near the helicotrema, and the narrow end is the part near the stapes.

paragraphs.text: At the wide end, the membrane has a **large mass,** labeled M, and a **small stiffness,** labeled k. This end is heavy and floppy.
paragraphs.plain: At the wide end, the membrane has a large mass, labeled M, and a small stiffness, labeled k. This end is heavy and floppy.

paragraphs.text: At the narrow end, the membrane has a **small mass,** labeled m, and a **large stiffness,** labeled K. This end is light and stiff.
paragraphs.plain: At the narrow end, the membrane has a small mass, labeled m, and a large stiffness, labeled K. This end is light and stiff.

paragraphs.text: Between the two ends, the mass gradually decreases and the stiffness gradually increases along the length of the membrane.
paragraphs.plain: Between the two ends, the mass gradually decreases and the stiffness gradually increases along the length of the membrane.

paragraphs.text: **Each spot on the membrane acts like its own mass-spring system.** Every small piece of the basilar membrane has its own mass and its own stiffness, so every piece has its own natural frequency of vibration. Perturbation theory tells us which way that frequency goes along the membrane.
paragraphs.plain: Each spot on the membrane acts like its own mass-spring system. Every small piece of the basilar membrane has its own mass and its own stiffness, so every piece has its own natural frequency of vibration. Perturbation theory tells us which way that frequency goes along the membrane.

paragraphs.text: At the heavy, floppy end, large mass lowers the frequency and small stiffness also lowers the frequency. Both effects push in the same direction, so this end vibrates at **low frequencies.**
paragraphs.plain: At the heavy, floppy end, large mass lowers the frequency and small stiffness also lowers the frequency. Both effects push in the same direction, so this end vibrates at low frequencies.

paragraphs.text: At the light, stiff end, small mass raises the frequency and large stiffness also raises the frequency. Both effects again push in the same direction, so this end vibrates at **high frequencies.**
paragraphs.plain: At the light, stiff end, small mass raises the frequency and large stiffness also raises the frequency. Both effects again push in the same direction, so this end vibrates at high frequencies.

paragraphs.text: Therefore **frequency increases steadily along the membrane,** from low frequencies at the heavy, floppy end to high frequencies at the light, stiff end.
paragraphs.plain: Therefore frequency increases steadily along the membrane, from low frequencies at the heavy, floppy end to high frequencies at the light, stiff end.

paragraphs.text: **A sound with many frequencies is sorted out by place.** When a sound containing several frequencies at once enters the cochlea, each frequency makes the part of the membrane tuned to that frequency vibrate the most. A low-frequency component shakes the heavy, floppy region, and a high-frequency component shakes the light, stiff region.

When a sound containing several frequencies at once enters the cochlea, each frequency makes the part of the membrane tuned to that frequency vibrate the most. A low-frequency component shakes the heavy, floppy region, and a high-frequency component shakes the light, stiff region.

paragraphs.text: A single complex sound, such as a vowel, is thus spread out along the membrane, with each of its frequencies causing strong vibration at its own location. How strongly each location vibrates reflects how strong that frequency is in the sound.

paragraphs.text: **Neurons along the membrane report the pattern to the brain.** Rows of **neurons** are attached along the length of the basilar membrane. When a region of the membrane vibrates, the neurons attached to that region send signals, and those signals travel **to the brain.**

paragraphs.text: The brain can tell which frequencies are present by noticing **which neurons are active,** since each neuron is connected to a location that responds to one particular frequency. It can tell how strong each frequency is by how strongly those neurons are signaling.

paragraphs.text: This is how the listener's brain can register "a high frequency of this much and a low frequency of this much." A pattern of activity at one set of locations corresponds to "scene," and a pattern at a different set of locations corresponds to "son."

paragraphs.text: **Georg von Békésy won the Nobel Prize in 1961** for his work on how the cochlea responds to sound. His work established that different frequencies cause the strongest vibration at different places along the basilar membrane, which is the mechanism that lets the ear separate a sound into its frequencies.

His work established that different frequencies cause the strongest vibration at different places along the basilar membrane, which is the mechanism that lets the ear separate a sound into its frequencies.

paragraphs.text: **The vocal folds are two small muscles in the throat.** Each vocal fold is about 1 **cm in length** and about 1 **mm in height.** The folds sit across the airway, and air from the lungs has to pass between them on its way up to the mouth.

paragraphs.text: In a camera view looking down the throat at the vocal folds during speech, the two folds meet along a line, and the gap between them appears as a narrow dark slit. That slit is the opening that air passes through, and it is the space that repeatedly opens and closes when the folds vibrate.

paragraphs.text: **Muscle has mass and stiffness, so the vocal folds behave like a mass-spring system.** Since a vocal fold has both mass and stiffness, it can oscillate just like the mass on a spring, and perturbation theory applies to it directly.

sections.title: Solving Differential Equations with Arithmetic, Python, and Software 1.0

paragraphs.text: **Euler's explicit method solves differential equations using arithmetic.** A **differential equation** is an equation about rates of change, like ẋ = v and v̇ = −(k/m) x . Euler's explicit method turns each of these into an update of the form x[n] = … dt + x[n − 1], where the new value equals the previous value plus a rate multiplied by a small time step.
paragraphs.plain: Euler's explicit method solves differential equations using arithmetic. A differential equation is an equation about rates of change, like ẋ = v and v̇ = −(k/m) x . Euler's explicit method turns each of these into an update of the form x[n] = … dt + x[n − 1], where the new value equals the previous value plus a rate multiplied by a small time step.

paragraphs.text: Every update is just multiplication and addition. By repeating these simple arithmetic steps many times, we can follow how a system like a mass on a spring moves through time, without any other kind of mathematics.
paragraphs.plain: Every update is just multiplication and addition. By repeating these simple arithmetic steps many times, we can follow how a system like a mass on a spring moves through time, without any other kind of mathematics.

paragraphs.text: The method is named for **Leonhard Euler,** the mathematician whose portrait appears alongside photographs of a woman and of her receiving a medal at a formal ceremony, honoring work carried out with arithmetic methods of this kind.
paragraphs.plain: The method is named for Leonhard Euler, the mathematician whose portrait appears alongside photographs of a woman and of her receiving a medal at a formal ceremony, honoring work carried out with arithmetic methods of this kind.

paragraphs.text: **The same stepping procedure is done in Python.** Computers are built to repeat arithmetic quickly and exactly, so a loop in Python can carry out the Euler updates for as many steps as we want. Each pass through the loop computes one new position and one new velocity and appends them to lists, just as in the two loops written for the harmonic oscillator.

paragraphs.text: A **dynamical system** is anything in the world whose state changes over time according to a rule. Examples include a spring, a cooling room, or a learning computer program. A **differential equation** is the mathematical way of writing down that rule. It does not directly tell us where something is. It tells us how fast it is changing and in what direction, given where it is right now.

A differential equation is the mathematical way of writing down that rule. It does not directly tell us where something is. It tells us how fast it is changing and in what direction, given where it is right now.

paragraphs.text: Once we know the rule for change, we can work out the whole history of the system, step by step, starting from a known starting point.
paragraphs.plain: Once we know the rule for change, we can work out the whole history of the system, step by step, starting from a known starting point.

paragraphs.text: This is why differential equations are called the **mathematical expression of dynamical systems.** The equation is the rule, and the system's behavior over time is what the rule produces.

paragraphs.text: In 1676, **Isaac Newton wrote a letter to Gottfried Leibniz** and hid one of his central ideas inside an **anagram.** An anagram in this sense is a scrambled set of letters that works like a code. Newton could send it, and later, once he had fully proven the idea, he could reveal what it said.

An anagram in this sense is a scrambled set of letters that works like a code. Newton could send it, and later, once he had fully proven the idea, he could reveal what it said.

sections.title: Inference and Learning in Neural Networks

paragraphs.text: A neural network works in two modes, **inference** and **learning,** and both rely on the inner product.
paragraphs.plain: A neural network works in two modes, inference and learning, and both rely on the inner product.

paragraphs.text: **Inference** is how the network makes a decision. We give the system a signal vector, and its weights are inner-producted with it. This is the **template matching** step. The result becomes a new representation, which is then inner-producted with the next set of weights, and this repeats **over and over** across many stages. This is the **hierarchical perception** step.

The result becomes a new representation, which is then inner-producted with the next set of weights, and this repeats over and over across many stages. This is the hierarchical perception step.

paragraphs.text: Each stage takes the previous stage's output as its input, much as V1 feeds V2 and V4 feeds TEO in the brain.
paragraphs.plain: Each stage takes the previous stage's output as its input, much as V1 feeds V2 and V4 feeds TEO in the brain.

paragraphs.text: The process runs step by step, **like Euler's algorithm.** Each step takes the current values, applies a fixed rule, and produces the next values, until the final probability distribution comes out at the end.

paragraphs.text: **Learning** is how the network gets good weights. We give the system a signal vector **whose identity we already know** and ask it to infer that identity using its **initial random w's.** With random weights, it cannot do this correctly, and its output does not match the correct answer.

paragraphs.text: Repeating this over many known examples gradually turns the random templates into templates that match real speech sounds and real faces, so that inference produces the right decision.

In the first, we are handed a huge number of pictures of faces, each made of about 48 **million pixels,** and we have to say which of 1000 **possible people** each face belongs to. In the second, we are handed **speech waves,** and for each wave we have to say which of 25 **sounds** it corresponds to. A neural network is the kind of system that can solve both of these problems.

sections.title: Two Huge Questions — Learning and Inference

paragraphs.text: Two big questions describe how a neural network works.
paragraphs.plain: Two big questions describe how a neural network works.

paragraphs.text: **Learning** asks how, specifically, a network learns its weights.
paragraphs.plain: Learning asks how, specifically, a network learns its weights.

paragraphs.text: **Inference** asks how, specifically, a network combines its weights with its inputs to produce an output.
paragraphs.plain: Inference asks how, specifically, a network combines its weights with its inputs to produce an output.

paragraphs.text: Inference is answered first, since inference is part of learning. Every round of learning begins with forward propagation, and forward propagation is inference. The network cannot measure its loss until it has combined the input with its current weights and produced an answer. So the exact calculation used in inference has to be understood before learning can be.

So the exact calculation used in inference has to be understood before learning can be.

sections.title: Two Beliefs About AI and the Brain

paragraphs.text: There are two opposing beliefs about how modern AI relates to the human mind. These are views, not exam material.
paragraphs.plain: There are two opposing beliefs about how modern AI relates to the human mind. These are views, not exam material.

paragraphs.text: Most engineers, neuroscientists, and people in general hold that modern AI has nothing to do with how humans think, perceive, act, or decide. On this view, the brain is full of chemistry, electrical activity, and abstract processes, and none of that is part of **large language models** (LLMs), which are made only of numbers and arithmetic.
paragraphs.plain: Most engineers, neuroscientists, and people in general hold that modern AI has nothing to do with how humans think, perceive, act, or decide. On this view, the brain is full of chemistry, electrical activity, and abstract processes, and none of that is part of large language models (LLMs), which are made only of numbers and arithmetic.

paragraphs.text: A smaller group, including Khalil Iskarous, holds that modern AI is the result of about 100 years of gradual, evolutionary tinkering with how arithmetic can **emulate the chemical and electrical activity of the brain.** On this view, those attempts appear to have succeeded, so the arithmetic in modern AI is a working imitation of brain activity rather than something unrelated to it.
